title: Blessed the womb (Luke 11:27–28)
hook: a woman praises his mother; he says blessed are they who hear the word and keep it; Catholics see Mary as both

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples asked to be taught to pray, and a man's importunity kept him knocking at midnight. Your line was knock.

A son gives a great speech at a wedding, and an aunt in the crowd calls out: your mother must be so proud! It's a compliment to him, routed through her. Something like that happens in Luke. Jesus is in the middle of a tense argument with people who say he heals by the power of devils. A woman in the crowd can't hold it in. She lifts up her voice and calls out a blessing on his mother. It's two verses long: what she said, and what he said back.
screen: `YOUR MOTHER MUST BE SO PROUD.` → `A VOICE FROM THE CROWD.` → `TWO VERSES LONG.`

segments.voice: Here's her cry in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the paps that gave thee suck." Paps is an old word for breasts. It's an earthy, motherly blessing, the kind women in that world gave: how happy the mother of such a son. Jesus answers: "Yea rather, blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it." Some people hear that as a brush-off of his mother. Catholics hear something else, and Luke gives the reason. When the angel came, Mary said be it done to me according to thy word. At Bethlehem, Luke says, Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. Elizabeth says to her, blessed art thou that hast believed. And in her own song, Mary says all generations shall call me blessed. So in Luke, Mary carries both blessings at once: she bore him, and she heard and kept the word. Augustine said it this way, in his own words: Mary was more blessed in receiving Christ by faith than in conceiving him in the flesh. Jesus takes a blessing only one woman in history could have, and opens it to everyone listening. Nobody else can be his mother. Anybody can hear and keep. That's why Catholics honor Mary as the first disciple, not only as a mother: she shows what keeping looks like.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE WOMB THAT BORE THEE.` · `YEA RATHER: HEAR AND KEEP.` · `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.` · `ONE COULD BEAR HIM; ALL CAN KEEP.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY WHO HEAR AND KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Let one of this week's lines choose you: go in peace, nothing for the journey, no looking back, peace be to this house, knock. Say it slowly inside a few times, the way Mary pondered, and don't analyze it; just keep it, like a stone in your pocket you keep touching. If you pray, ask to keep it the way she did.
Blessed the womb. A woman's cry from the crowd praising Jesus' mother, and his answer: blessed are those who hear the word and keep it, as Mary did. Today's word.

Your line: hear and keep it. That's week sixty-six: she loved much, the women who funded him, take nothing, he set his face, the seventy-two, teach us to pray, and the womb. Day four hundred sixty-two, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholics read Luke 11:27–28 on some feasts and Saturday Masses of Our Lady, and many pray the rosary as a way of pondering the Gospel's words with Mary.

fork.setup: a woman in the crowd calls out a blessing on your mother. how does Jesus answer?
options: say rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.
say his mother isn't to be praised.
fork.reveal: he widens the blessing to everyone who hears and keeps the word, and Luke has already shown Mary doing exactly that.

original.note: Greek: blessed, happy, the beatitude word. The woman uses it of the womb, and Jesus answers with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus brushed off a compliment to his mother.
what it means: he opens a blessing only Mary could have to everyone who hears and keeps the word, which Luke shows Mary doing too.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses keep (phylasso, and at Bethlehem syntereo) to tie Mary to the ideal hearer; menounge, yea rather, can mean yes, and even more.
recall: Latin: now you dismiss, Simeon's song

chat.says: Jesus said "blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it." Who's that about?
options: Anyone who hears and keeps it, and Mary first of all; she did both.
Only Mary, since she alone could bear him and be his mother.
Only the twelve apostles, who heard him teach every single day.
chat.meaning: Nobody else can be his mother, but anybody can hear and keep; Luke shows Mary doing both, so Catholics call her the first disciple.
